overall_session_summary: Across 34 turns, you demonstrated consistently empathic, professional communication with clear validation, normalization, and permission-asking. You built strong trust (including an early confidentiality review) and elicited rich narratives about mood lability, emptiness, interpersonal instability, fear of abandonment, identity disturbance, impulsivity, anger dysregulation, stress-related paranoia/dissociation, trauma exposure, hyperarousal, anxiety, and substance use. You pivoted appropriately to suicide risk mid-visit and maintained a collaborative tone through the close with homework assigned. Performance progressed from Emerging early to stable Proficient thereafter. Primary gaps were structural: no explicit agenda or expectations were set; focused assessment and risk wrap-up were incomplete (intent/plan/means, HI, protective factors, mania screen, sleep specifics, prior treatments/meds/allergies, family history); and a concise summary with a working differential was never shared. Sessions were weighted toward rapport and phenomenology at the expense of synthesis and concrete planning.

Introduction and Building Rapport.strengths: Warm, validating tone; clear confidentiality review; permission-asking; normalization; explicit invitation for process feedback; consistent efforts to reduce perceived invalidation.
Introduction and Building Rapport.weaknesses: No explicit agenda or elicitation of expectations; excessive time spent on rapport without transitioning to structure, synthesis, and planning.

Open-Ended Inquiry.strengths: Effective open invitations once initiated (e.g., elaborating on emptiness, relationships), allowing meaningful narratives that deepened the HPI.
Open-Ended Inquiry.weaknesses: Delayed initial open-ended question; occasional leading/closed phrasing; limited summarizing before transitioning to focused probes.

Focused Inquiry and Probing Questions.strengths: Appropriate and progressive probing of triggers, duration, interpersonal patterns, anger, impulsivity, dissociation, trauma, anxiety, hyperarousal, and substance use.
Focused Inquiry and Probing Questions.weaknesses: Key domains remained incomplete: full suicide risk (intent/plan/means, protective factors), homicidal ideation, brief mania/bipolar screen, sleep specifics, prior treatments/medications/allergies, family psychiatric history (including bipolar), concise functional impact; timing and efficiency of probes could improve.

Differential Diagnosis Development.strengths: Appropriate deferral early while gathering history.
Differential Diagnosis Development.weaknesses: No concise summary or working differential was shared despite adequate data (e.g., emotion dysregulation with borderline traits/disorder; trauma-related symptoms/PTSD; rule out bipolar spectrum; MDD with mood lability). No explicit differentiation of reactive affective shifts vs sustained hypomania/mania, and no shared reasoning with the patient.

Communication Skills and Professionalism.strengths: Consistently empathic, clear, nonjudgmental, and collaborative; good normalization and permission-asking; language tailored to a validation-sensitive patient; respectful closure.
Communication Skills and Professionalism.weaknesses: Occasional typos and occasional leading phrasing; could pair direct risk questions more consistently with normalization/validation.

Motivation/Counseling.strengths: Reflective listening; affirmations; process transparency; homework invitation; collaborative stance; elicited goals for stability near the end.
Motivation/Counseling.weaknesses: Limited elicitation of change talk, goals, and values early; minimal concrete coping skills or safety planning delivered in-session; did not explore prior unhelpful treatment experiences before proposing plan.

things_you_do_well: Establish trust quickly with clear confidentiality framing and empathic validation.
Use permission-asking and normalization to reduce defensiveness on sensitive topics.
Elicit rich narratives with well-timed open-ended prompts once initiated.
Maintain a calm, respectful, and collaborative tone throughout, including wrap-up.
Address suicide risk directly and professionally.
things_you_should_do_less_of: Spending multiple turns on rapport without setting a clear agenda or expectations.
Prolonged phenomenology without timely synthesis, risk wrap-up, and planning.
Leading or closed questions when an open prompt or summary would yield better data.
Deferring diagnostic formulation until the end (or not sharing one at all).
Letting minor typos and phrasing drift (which can read as inattention to detail).
recommendations: Open with structure in the first 60–90 seconds: elicit the patient’s priorities, set a brief agenda (history, safety, summary/differential, plan), and confirm expectations.

Complete a concise, structured risk screen early and revisit briefly before closing: current/past SI (passive vs active), intent, plan, means, past attempts and NSSI, protective factors, and homicidal ideation.

Rapidly close key diagnostic screens: brief bipolar screen (4+ days elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity); sleep/energy; substance use (last 30 days, type/amount/frequency); prior treatments/medications/allergies and responses; family psychiatric history (especially bipolar); concise functional impact.

Summarize and share a working differential mid-to-late visit: likely emotion dysregulation with borderline traits/disorder and trauma-related symptoms; rule out bipolar spectrum; consider MDD with mood lability. Distinguish reactive mood shifts from sustained hypomanic/manic episodes. Check understanding and invite questions.
Use brief summaries to transition between open-ended exploration and focused probes, signaling why you’re asking each cluster of questions.
Enhance MI: reflect nervousness/hope, explore what was unhelpful in prior care and what the patient wants done differently, elicit values and concrete goals, and collaboratively select next steps.
Deliver at least one in-session skill and a micro–safety plan: teach a quick grounding or paced-breathing exercise; identify early warning signs, coping steps, and crisis resources; confirm buy-in.
Reduce leading phrasing; prefer open prompts first, then tighten with targeted probes. Pair direct risk questions with normalization (e.g., “I ask everyone because your safety matters”).

Close with structure every time: a 30–60 second synthesis, explicit differential and rationale, confirm risk status and crisis resources, SMART between-session task(s), and clear next-step expectations.
Document clearly: risk assessment details (intent/plan/means/protective factors), differential reasoning, and the collaborative plan (skills/homework, referrals such as DBT, follow-up cadence).
